title: HYPOTHESIS: candidate genetic routes to the four changes a powered-flying fish would need
status: HYPOTHESIS THROUGHOUT. Not a predicted genome, not a design, and not a claim that any of this is achievable.
constraint: A draft genome of a flying fish EXISTS and is annotated, so the limit here is not missing genes. Xu et al. 2021 (Front Genet 12:695700, doi 10.3389/fgene.2021.695700) assembled the mirrorwing flyingfish Hirundichthys speculiger and predicted 23,611 protein-coding genes, of which 23,492 (99.5%) carry at least one database hit; that assembly is the one catalogued as GCA_018398805.1. What the flying fish lacks is PHENOTYPE and EXPRESSION records: that paper reports no RNA-seq and no transcriptome at all, no mutant, no kinetics and no regulatory network, and ZFIN-style expression and mutant-phenotype data exist only for zebrafish and, through Bgee, medaka. Every gene link in this map is therefore a PROXY-species record, zebrafish (Danio rerio) or medaka (Oryzias latipes, the same order Beloniformes as flying fish), and it is a proxy for that reason rather than because flying-fish genes are unknown. None of these links is a flying-fish measurement. No bird data is used anywhere: class Aves is this project's held-out clade, so bird flight-muscle and respiratory genetics are excluded by construction.

summary.honest_reading: No requirement has a route that reaches it. Three of the four are 'partial', and in each case the partial route answers a different question from the one asked: for the fin, a 1.65-fold area increase against the 3.9-fold required, with span and aspect ratio never measured at all; for the muscle, an increment on existing trunk muscle rather than an allocation to the pectoral fin, which no manipulation has ever been shown to enlarge; for air breathing, an anatomy that living fishes have evolved at least nine times over but whose construction genetics is mostly correlative and entirely absent for the flying fish's own order. Oxygen delivery is a flat 'none', and the Lean thread's kernel-checked elimination puts the shortfall at about 26-fold on a product of three physiological quantities that genetics does not report. The useful result of this exercise is the map of where the biology is missing, not a buildable design.

items.requirement: pectoral lifting area about 3.9 times the real fish's and span about 2.5 times, at a similar aspect ratio
items.verdict: This is the ONE item with real genetic routes, because fin proportion is the trait this project studied. But no route reaches the required magnitude: the largest measured increase in pectoral fin area from any single manipulation is +65% of wild type (hhip loss of function at 72 hours post fertilisation), and the requirement is +290%, a 3.9-fold area. Nothing in the fetched literature multiplies a fin's area by 3.9, and no manipulation was measured as a span or an aspect ratio at all, so the shape requirement has no sourced route even where the size one partly does. Combining levers is untested: the one double mutant that changes fin proportion (kcnh2a with lat4a) redistributes size between fins rather than scaling one fin up.

items.requirement: a large aerobic pectoral flight muscle at about 16% of body mass, where the real fish has small fin muscles

bat_comparison.source: PMC10966098 (Onychonycteris paper, 10.1038/s42003-024-06032-9) citing Bullen and McKenzie 2004: flight muscle on average 9.13 % of body mass in extant bats, minimum 7.8 %

items.verdict: PARTIAL for 'more muscle', NONE for 'a pectoral muscle at 16% of body mass'. Myostatin loss of function is a real, repeated, quantified genetic route to extra skeletal muscle in teleosts: 16% more skeletal muscle in a CRISPR mstn-knockout red sea bream breed, 21% higher body weight in TALEN mstnb-/- zebrafish, 29.7% higher body weight with more muscle cells in CRISPR MSTN channel catfish, 41% more back muscle in male CRISPR MSTN olive flounder, and significant gains in medaka, common carp and antisense-knockdown Nile tilapia. Four reasons it does not reach the requirement. (i) Every one of these is an INCREMENT on existing muscle, not an allocation: the red sea bream '16%' is a 16% increase in total skeletal muscle, which is not the same quantity as a muscle equal to 16% of body mass, and no fetched source reports pectoral fin muscle as a fraction of body mass in any fish. (ii) Every one of these is axial/trunk muscle. No fetched source reports mstn loss, or any other manipulation, enlarging the pectoral fin musculature; the only fin-muscle genetics found (met, six1a/b, six4a/b, tbx5, lbx1) is loss-of-function reducing fin muscle, with no gain-of-function in the other direction. (iii) The mstn effect in fish is predominantly hyperplastic and the link from fibre number to mass is not reliable: transgenic dominant-negative MSTN medaka doubled muscle fibre number with gross muscle mass unaltered, and the authors state MSTN loss of function failed to induce double-muscling in medaka. (iv) The side effects are concentrated exactly where a flight muscle needs support: short body and small centrum in red sea bream, fewer and shorter vertebrae in yellow catfish mstnb knockouts, and fat accumulating inside the muscle in zebrafish and tilapia. For scale, the most aerobically specialised teleost measured here, juvenile Pacific bluefin tuna, carries only 3.77-10.69% of body mass as red muscle in total, over the whole body.

items.verdict: NONE. Three findings, all negative for the requirement. (1) Capacity: every fetched genetic result on fish globins runs downward. Icefishes lost both haemoglobin gene clusters through transposable-element-mediated deletion; Asian noodlefishes lost myoglobin outright and let haemoglobin, haptoglobin and hemogen deteriorate; Antarctic notothenioids reduced haemoglobin multiplicity to a single adult isoform with lower oxygen affinity; the icefish candidate gene FAAP20 is associated with LOW haematocrit. The zebrafish globin loci and their LCR give a well-mapped cis-regulatory handle (two loci, two developmental switches, GATA1/NFE2 motifs, reporter-confirmed LCR), and the Root effect is a demonstrated pH-driven unloading mechanism in fish swimbladders, but no fetched source reports any manipulation that RAISES blood oxygen capacity in a fish. (2) Pump: genetic routes to a bigger fish heart do exist, which is the one real positive here. Knockdown of miR-458-3p and miR-144-5p drives cardiomyocyte proliferation and enlarged heart development through bmp2 in an Antarctic icefish, and Tg(myl7:ATF3) zebrafish develop cardiac hypertrophy with increased cardiac cell proliferation. But the icefish route is compensation for having no haemoglobin at all, the zebrafish route is pathological (fibrosis, disorganised sarcomeres, long-QT-like dysfunction), and neither reports a rise in cardiac output or oxygen delivery. (3) Magnitude: measured fish performance is not close. The highest fetched fish maximum oxygen uptake is 781.31 +/- 16.50 mg O2 kg-1 h-1 with a maximum cardiac output of 69.12 +/- 2.39 ml min-1 kg-1 in schoolmaster snapper, i.e. roughly 9 ml O2 kg-1 min-1 by this agent's arithmetic, reached by raising heart rate and tissue extraction rather than stroke volume, and the fish envelope plateaus at about 1.75-fold resting cardiac output and 2.5-fold extraction in salmon and tilapia on warming. No fish in any fetched source approaches the per-kilogram oxygen delivery the physics thread asks for. I deliberately fetched no mammalian baseline, so the exact multiple belongs to the physics thread; the point for this thread is that the shortfall is not marginal and that no genetic route in the fetched literature addresses it.

items.verdict: Real fishes breathe air by at least 9 distinct routes, so the ANATOMY is not hypothetical at all: this is the one requirement of the four that living fishes already meet, repeatedly and in several unrelated lineages. The GENETICS is a different matter. 8 of the 9 routes have some genetics attached, but only 2 rise above correlation to a functional result, so for most routes the molecular account of how the surface is built is not available. And the decisive fact for this project: NOTHING is known for Beloniformes, the order containing flying fishes, halfbeaks and needlefishes, and nothing at all for Exocoetidae. The homology of the gas bladder and the tetrapod lung is accepted and now supported at the level of cell types, but the molecular account of the switch between them is incomplete and partly negative, so even the best-studied starting point does not give a route.

routes.route: respiratory gas bladder / physostomous swim bladder used as a lung
routes.anatomy: The gas bladder, a gas-filled diverticulum of the anterior foregut that buds dorsally, is retained as a respiratory organ rather than repurposed for buoyancy. In Arapaima gigas it is a 'gigantic, highly vascularized air-breathing organ (ABO)' whose wall is filled by proliferating parenchyma; in Pangasianodon hypophthalmus it is a 'highly trabeculated respiratory swim-bladder'; in the erythrinid jeju 'the anterior section of the posterior bladder is highly vascularized'. The air-blood barrier is extremely thin (harmonic mean 0.22 um in juvenile A. gigas) compared with the gill water-blood barrier (9.61 um).
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Both occur. Arapaima gigas is 'one of the very few obligate air-breathing fish' and is an obligate air breather from a few weeks post hatch; Hoplerythrinus unitaeniatus, Pangasianodon hypophthalmus and Chitala ornata are facultative, breathing air mainly in hypoxic water. Hoplias malabaricus has the same two-chambered physostomous bladder but uses it only for buoyancy.

genetics.what_is_shown: Genetics exists for how a gas bladder is BUILT, not for how a buoyancy bladder is converted into a respiratory one. Funk et al. compared lung and gas-bladder budding and found 'during gas bladder development, Nkx2.1 and Sox2 expression are inconsistent with the hypothesis that they regulate the direction of gas bladder budding', that 'During gas bladder development, Bmp4 is not expressed', and that the Actinopteri-restricted paralogue Bmp16 'is expressed dorsally in the developing gas bladder of bowfin', leading them to hypothesise that 'Bmp16 was recruited to regulate gas bladder development in the Actinopteri in place of Bmp4' (expression only; bichir, bowfin, zebrafish). Zheng et al. RNA-seq of the zebrafish swimbladder identified 'prominent transcription factor genes in the swimbladder including hoxc4a, hoxc6a, hoxc8a and foxf1' and confirmed their embryonic swimbladder expression. For the surfactant lining, Chen et al. showed in zebrafish that 'bloc1s1 is highly expressed in the swimbladder during postembryonic stages and is required for positively regulating the expression of the genes, which is known to govern surfactant production and lung development in mammals', identifying 'BLOS1 as a crucial regulator of the surfactant system' (mutant lines, so necessity for the surfactant gene programme). Protein-level work shows the surfactant itself: in eel and perch 'Western blot analysis using specific antibodies to human surfactant protein A (SP-A) showed a cross-reaction with swim bladder tissue homogenate proteins', and in carp an anti-SP-A antibody 'bound on Western blots to proteins present in intestinal mucosa and in swim bladder, but not in gills'. NO gene, regulatory change or developmental route is known that makes a gas bladder respiratory rather than buoyant, and none is known for any of the respiratory-gas-bladder taxa above (Arapaima, Heterotis, Pangasianodon, Chitala, Hoplerythrinus); all the molecular work listed here is on buoyancy swimbladders of zebrafish, carp, eel and perch or on budding direction in bichir/bowfin.
genetics.organism: Danio rerio (swimbladder transcriptome, bloc1s1 mutants), Polypterus (bichir), Amia calva (bowfin), Cyprinus carpio, Anguilla anguilla, Perca fluviatilis
genetics.experiment_type: in situ hybridisation / expression survey, RNA-seq, zebrafish mutant lines (CRISPR/TALEN), Western blot, immunohistochemistry, cell culture

costs_and_limits: BUOYANCY CONFLICT, stated directly: 'Using the swimbladder as a buoyancy structure resulted in the loss of its function as an air-breathing organ and required the development of a gas secreting mechanism' (Pelster 2021). The two jobs are mutually exclusive in the erythrinids: the jeju uses the bladder for aerial respiration, the sister genus traira 'uses the swimbladder as a buoyancy organ and not for aerial oxygen uptake'.

A gas bladder is a poor buoyancy device away from the surface: 'on descend from the water surface its contribution as a buoyancy device is very limited because the swimbladder is compressed by increasing hydrostatic pressure' (Pelster 2021).

Volume control is slow: 'Gas secretion as well as gas resorption are slow phenomena, so that rapid changes in depth cannot instantaneously be compensated by appropriate volume changes' (Pelster 2021).
Both uses require surfactant: 'As gas-filled cavities the respiratory swimbladder and the buoyancy device require surfactant' (Pelster 2021).

Oxidative cost: 'Due to high oxygen partial pressures inside the bladder air-exposed tissues need an effective reactive oxygen species defense system' (Pelster 2021). In the air-breathing jeju, which experiences variable bladder PO2, 'only a reduced responsiveness of the ROS defense system to changing environmental PO2 was detected'.

GILL REDUCTION AND ITS KNOCK-ON COSTS: 'To avoid the loss of oxygen to hypoxic water at the gills many air-breathing fish show a reduced gill surface area. This, in turn, also reduces surface area available for other functions, so that breathing air is connected to a number of physiological adjustments with respect to ion homeostasis, acid-base regulation and nitrogen excretion' (Pelster 2021). In developing Arapaima this shows as 'a reduction in gill lamellar surface area, increase in gill diffusion distance, and proliferation of the parenchyma in the ABO', compensated by rising ionocyte density.

CO2 EXCRETION STAYS AQUATIC: aerial CO2 excretion is only 3-12% of total in Arapaima under normocapnia, and 'Because of the much greater diffusion constant of CO2 than O2 in water, the gills also remain important for CO2 release' (Fernandes 2012). Chitala ornata still excretes 79% and Pangasianodon 91% of CO2 to severely hypoxic water. The ABO can take over CO2 excretion (59-71% of total) only when the water itself is hypercapnic.

The feared branchial O2 loss turns out to be small: 'the proposed branchial oxygen loss in air-breathing fish is likely only a minor inefficiency' (4.9% in Pangasianodon, 3% in Chitala), so gill reduction is not forced by O2 loss alone.

sources.quote: Using the swimbladder as a buoyancy structure resulted in the loss of its function as an air-breathing organ and required the development of a gas secreting mechanism.

The average respiratory surface area of the swim bladder (2173 cm² kg⁻¹) exceeded that of the gills (780 cm² kg⁻¹) by a factor of 2.79. Due to the extremely thin air-blood barrier in the swim bladder (harmonic mean 0.22 μm) and the much thicker water-blood barrier of the gills (9.61 μm), the morphometric diffusing capacity for oxygen and carbon dioxide was 88 times greater in the swim bladder than in the gills.

routes.route: true ventral lung (paired or unpaired), retained from the ancestral bony-fish condition
routes.anatomy: A gas-filled organ budding VENTRALLY from the anterior foregut, with an alveolar or trabecular parenchyma, its own pulmonary arterial supply, and in lungfish an alveolar epithelium. 'lungs are described in actinopterygian polypterids and in all sarcopterygians, including coelacanths and lungfish'. The lungfish lung carries a distinct 'alveolar epithelium cell' type in single-cell data. Coelacanths have a pulmonary vasculature; in fossil latimerioids the lung was ossified and may also have served hearing.
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Obligate in lungfish: 'African dipnoi (Protopterus sp.) are obligate air-breathing fish'. Bichirs and reedfish are facultative air breathers with functional gills. Latimeria's lung is reduced/fatty in the extant form; the respiratory role is inferred for the fossils.

genetics.what_is_shown: A single-cell transcriptome atlas of the West African lungfish respiratory system defines the cell types of a fish lung and their change during terrestrialization: 'Lung alveolar epithelial genes upregulated in terrestrialized lungfish included npc2 (NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 2) ... and the antioxidant enzyme genes mgst1 (microsomal glutathione S-transferase 1) and prdx1 (peroxiredoxin-1)'. For lung DEVELOPMENT in a ray-finned fish lung, Funk et al. found the tetrapod programme conserved: 'Nkx2.1 and Sox2 show reciprocal dorsoventral expression patterns during tetrapod lung development and are important regulators of lung budding; their expression during bichir lung development is conserved' and 'Bmp4 is expressed ventrally during lung development in bichir'. This is expression and correlation only; no gene has been knocked out or overexpressed in a lungfish, bichir or coelacanth.
genetics.experiment_type: scRNA-seq, cross-species integration, in situ hybridisation / expression survey

costs_and_limits: Air exposure dries and remodels the integument even in an obligate lung breather: in aestivating Protopterus dolloi 'short-term aestivation induces major reorganization, with narrowing of epidermal layers and decrease of mucous cells', and 'aestivation correlates with an increased oxidative stress and changes of Heat Shock Proteins expression'.

Reliance on a lung did not by itself produce a divided circulation: the lungfish-grade solution still returns ABO blood through a single heart (see Monopterus/Electrophorus entries for the explicit test of this).

The coelacanth lung is dual-purpose rather than purely respiratory: 'the lung of extinct coelacanths supported both respiratory and auditory functions', a second instance of one gas-filled organ being asked to do two jobs.

sources.quote: Lung alveolar epithelial genes upregulated in terrestrialized lungfish included npc2 (NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 2), which has a role in lung lipid metabolism and is associated with Niemann–Pick disease characterized by alveolar proteinosis, and the antioxidant enzyme genes mgst1 (microsomal glutathione S-transferase 1) and prdx1 (peroxiredoxin-1)

African dipnoi (Protopterus sp.) are obligate air-breathing fish that, during dry season, may experience a period of dormancy named aestivation. Aestivation is characterized by complete reliance on pulmonary breathing

routes.route: suprabranchial chamber housing a gill-derived arborescent or labyrinthine respiratory organ
routes.anatomy: A pouch dorsal to the gill arches, lined with vascularised respiratory epithelium, into which gill-arch derivatives (arborescent 'respiratory trees' in Clarias, fan-like plates in Channa) project. Jiang et al. treat the suprabranchial chamber as 'the aerial breathing organ (suprabranchial chamber)' in contrast to 'the aquatic breathing organ (gill)'. The chamber's transcriptome is enriched for angiogenesis and elastic-fibre formation, consistent with 'its highly vascularized and elastic structure'.
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Facultative to strongly air-dependent. Channa striata is described in the indexed literature as an 'obligate air-breathing fish'; Clarias species are facultative but can walk overland and 'survive a considerable period without water'.

genetics.what_is_shown: Transcriptome comparisons of the gill against the suprabranchial chamber identify the programme as vascular and matrix-building rather than respiratory-protein-based: 'A gene pathway analysis concluded that four functional categories were significant, of which angiogenesis and elastic fibre formation were up-regulated in the suprabranchial chamber, indicating that the aerial breathing organ may be more efficient for gas exchange due to its highly vascularized and elastic structure. In contrast, ion uptake and transport and acid-base balance were up-regulated in the gill'. The specific genes vegf and fgfr were named for this organ in a cited Channa argus transcriptome. A Clarias gariepinus full-length (Iso-Seq) transcriptome spanning the ABO, gills, liver, skin and muscle reports that 'transcription factors such as zf-C2H2, Homeobox, bHLH, and MYB could underpin the African sharptooth catfish's developmental plasticity'. Genome-wide, Clarias magur shows expansion of 207 gene families and genes for 'urea cycle, vision, locomotion, olfactory and vomeronasal receptors, immune system, anti-microbial properties, mucus, thermoregulation, osmoregulation, air-breathing, detoxification'. All of this is expression, selection-scan or gene-family counting. NOTHING has been knocked out or overexpressed for this route; no gene is known to be necessary or sufficient for suprabranchial-chamber formation.
genetics.organism: Channa argus, Clarias gariepinus, Clarias magur
genetics.experiment_type: RNA-seq (gill vs ABO), Ka/Ks selection scan, PacBio Iso-Seq, whole-genome assembly and CAFE gene-family analysis

costs_and_limits: The division of labour is explicit and one-sided: 'ion uptake and transport and acid-base balance were up-regulated in the gill, indicating that the aquatic breathing organ functions in ion homeostasis and acid-base balance, in addition to breathing'. The ABO does not take those jobs over, so the gills cannot simply be given up.
The chamber is a wet cavity: it must stay moist to work, and no source read here reports a Channa or Clarias suprabranchial chamber functioning when the fish is fully dried.

sources.quote: angiogenesis and elastic fibre formation were up-regulated in the suprabranchial chamber, indicating that the aerial breathing organ may be more efficient for gas exchange due to its highly vascularized and elastic structure. In contrast, ion uptake and transport and acid-base balance were up-regulated in the gill

it was found that transcription factors such as zf-C2H2, Homeobox, bHLH, and MYB could underpin the African sharptooth catfish's developmental plasticity and its capacity to adapt its morphology and function to its environment.

routes.anatomy: A folded, highly vascularised ossified-plate organ derived from the first gill arch (epibranchial), sitting in a chamber above the gills. Huang & Lin treat it as 'an accessory air-breathing organ (the labyrinth organ)' and report 'morphological and functional specializations between the 1st and 4th gills in the genus Trichogaster', the 4th gill being 'generally much-reduced compared to the other gills'.
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Both occur within the suborder, and the contrast is documented in one experiment: 'the facultative air breather the Siamese fighting fish (Betta splendens) and the obligate air breathing blue gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus)'. Trichogaster microlebis died at higher rates when air breathing was blocked: 'Mortality in the restricted group was higher than those in the control and the hypoxic groups'.

genetics.what_is_shown: Only protein abundance measured by Western blot, and only as a response to oxygen treatment, not as a cause of the organ: 'the relative abundance of CAII was significantly increased only in the labyrinth organ in the hypoxic group compared to the control group on day 3' and 'The relative abundance of proliferating cell nuclear antigen also was significantly increased in the 1st gill, 4th gill and the labyrinth organ in the restricted group compared to the control group on day 14'. NO gene, transcription factor, regulatory element or developmental pathway is known for the formation of a labyrinth organ in any anabantoid. The only developmental study found is morphometric, not molecular, and its own conclusion is non-genetic: 'These differential larval responses to hypoxic rearing suggest that different larval habitats and activity levels are greater factors influencing developmental plasticity than genetic closeness of the two species.' This is the best-characterised air-breathing organ anatomically and one of the worst genetically.
genetics.organism: Trichogaster microlepis (protein), Betta splendens and Trichopodus trichopterus (morphometry only)
genetics.experiment_type: Western blot of CAII / NKA / PCNA, gill and labyrinth morphometry under chronic hypoxia and air-breathing restriction

costs_and_limits: Blocking access to air kills these fish faster than hypoxia itself does: 'Mortality in the restricted group was higher than those in the control and the hypoxic groups' (normoxic water, air breathing denied).

The organ is grown at the expense of the gills: the obligate air breather has gills roughly a third the area of its facultative relative's, and in the facultative species severe hypoxia cut branchial surface area by about 40% while mild hypoxia grew the labyrinth by 30%.
The labyrinth is a wet folded surface inside a chamber; no source read here reports it working in a desiccating environment, and no diffusion-capacity figure for it was found.

sources.quote: the relative abundance of CAII was significantly increased only in the labyrinth organ in the hypoxic group compared to the control group on day 3

Surface area of the emerging labyrinth, the air breathing organ, was ~ 85% larger in normoxic B. splendens compared to T. trichopterus. ... Mild, but not severe, hypoxia increased labyrinth surface area by 30% in B. splendens.

routes.route: posterior intestine used as an air-breathing organ (intestinal / gastrointestinal air breathing)
routes.anatomy: The hindgut epithelium is remodelled into a respiratory surface: it is 'highly modified, being well vascularized with intraepithelial capillaries, which makes it well suited for gas exchange', with a blood-gas diffusion distance comparable to that of the loach barbel. The digestive tract is partitioned: 'the digestive tract is divided into five functional regions, i.e., esophagus, anterior intestine, middle intestine, posterior intestine and rectum', the posterior region being the respiratory zone. Membrane fluidity of the posterior intestine is low, 'suggesting low permeability'.
taxa: Danio rerio (used as the KO comparison for the pathway)
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Facultative: 'The weatherloach, Misgurnus anguillicaudatus, is a facultative air-breathing teleost fish, which employs its partial digestive tract as an accessory respiratory organ.'

genetics.what_is_shown: This is the only air-breathing route in fishes with genetics at mechanism grade. Sun et al. identified mex3a as a positively selected gene in the air-breathing loach versus the non-air-breathing Triplophysa tibetana, then tested it in both directions: 'Deletion of Mex3a impaired loach air-breathing capacity by inhibiting angiogenesis through its interaction with T-box transcription factor 20. Mex3a overexpression significantly promoted angiogenesis. Structural analysis and point mutation revealed the critical role of the 201st amino acid in loach Mex3a for angiogenesis.' Knockouts lose vessels and die sooner in air: 'the deletion of the mex3a gene suppressed the formation of blood vessels in the posterior intestine of the loach, consequently diminishing the survival time of KO loach exposed to air'; 'the air-breathing frequency of KO loach was significantly lower than that of WT loach, and the oxygen consumption in the water was markedly higher'. The pathway was placed: 'Our findings suggested that Mex3a interacted with Tbx20 to regulate angiogenesis in fish via the Tbx20-Prok2-Prokr1 pathway', and the 201st residue 'underwent positive selection and mutation, evolving into asparagine (N), which was different from serine (S) in zebrafish'. Independently, Loxl2b knockout loach have better respiratory capacity: 'the deletion of Loxl2b obviously inhibited PI3K-AKT and TGF-beta signaling, meanwhile, induced VEGF signaling, which could cause vasodilation and angiogenesis to improve the air-breathing ability of loach'. Expression-level work supplies the rest: a six-stage developmental transcriptome of the posterior intestine mined '15 key pathways and 25 key genes', an air-breathing-inhibition experiment flagged 'fn1, ACE, EGFR, Pxdn, SDF, HIF, VEGF, SLC2A1, SLC5A8', and nutrient-transporter work found 'The presence of SGLT1 transcripts in the respiratory zone of the intestine suggests an overlap in function. However, in the case of PEPT1a, the distal limit was the midgut.'
genetics.organism: Misgurnus anguillicaudatus (CRISPR knockout and overexpression), with Danio rerio and mouse used by the authors to test the same pathway
genetics.experiment_type: positive-selection scan, haplotype-resolved genome assembly, CRISPR/Cas9 knockout, overexpression, point mutation, co-immunoprecipitation / protein interaction, immunofluorescence, TEM, qPCR, Western blot, RNA-seq, air-exposure survival, respirometry, Ussing chamber pharmacology, semi-quantitative RT-PCR

costs_and_limits: DIGESTION-RESPIRATION CONFLICT, the gut analogue of the buoyancy conflict: 'Results obtained here suggested an overlap of air-breathing and nutrient uptake function of posterior intestine in loach. Intestinal air-breathing inhibition in loach would influence the posterior intestine's nutrient uptake ability and endothelial capillary structure stability.' PEPT1a is absent from the respiratory hindgut altogether, so peptide uptake is given up in the respiratory zone.
Blocking air breathing damages the organ: in the inhibited group 'Intraepithelial capillaries in posterior intestines of loaches from T05 were broken'.

Nitrogen handling is displaced to the anterior gut: 'although the posterior intestine is highly modified for gas exchange, it is the anterior intestine that is the likely site of ammonia excretion and alkalinization leading to ammonia volatilization in the gut'.
No source read here reports CO2 excretion through the fish hindgut; CO2 remains a gill function in this route as in the others.

sources.quote: Deletion of Mex3a impaired loach air-breathing capacity by inhibiting angiogenesis through its interaction with T-box transcription factor 20. Mex3a overexpression significantly promoted angiogenesis. Structural analysis and point mutation revealed the critical role of the 201st amino acid in loach Mex3a for angiogenesis.

a posterior intestine (an ABO) transcriptome analysis revealed that the deletion of Loxl2b obviously inhibited PI3K-AKT and TGF-β signaling, meanwhile, induced VEGF signaling, which could cause vasodilation and angiogenesis to improve the air-breathing ability of loach

routes.route: stomach or gastric diverticulum used as an air-breathing organ
routes.anatomy: A thin-walled, vascularised stomach or an outpocketing (diverticulum) of it, with 'the air-blood diffusion barrier of the stomach' thinner than the gill water-blood barrier. In Otocinclus affinis the respiratory specialisation is framed as epithelial remodelling: 'regional localization of respiratory function in gut air-breathing fishes seems to be connected with "morphological remodeling" of the epithelium of their gut', giving 'the potential possibility to create an air-blood barrier in the gastrointestinal tract allowing gas diffusion'.
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Facultative: 'Pterygoplichthys anisitsi, a facultative air-breathing fish'; 'facultative gut air breathing fish species'.

genetics.what_is_shown: A single gene, measured as expression only, and offered as a marker of epithelial remodelling rather than a cause: 'The intensity of band fluorescence corresponding to the EGFR gene expression level is significantly higher in the stomach than in the diverticulum. Further, quantitative analysis of EGFR protein abundance also revealed its higher synthesis in the stomach than in the diverticulum and the immunohistochemistry method confirmed these results.' No loss- or gain-of-function experiment, no developmental pathway, and no genome- or transcriptome-wide study of a gastric air-breathing organ was found. This route's genetics is essentially a single correlative observation.

costs_and_limits: The stomach is a worse gas exchanger than the gills on paper and is used only when water breathing fails: 'Under severe hypoxic conditions, O2 uptake by the stomach is more efficient than by the gills, although the stomach has a much lower diffusing capacity. Thus, P. anisitsi uses gills under normoxic conditions but the stomach may also support aerobic metabolism depending on environmental conditions.'
A stomach full of air is a stomach not full of food; the digestive conflict documented for the loach hindgut applies by the same logic, but no source read here measured it for a gastric air breather.
No CO2 figure for a gastric air-breathing organ was found in any source read.

sources.quote: Under severe hypoxic conditions, O2 uptake by the stomach is more efficient than by the gills, although the stomach has a much lower diffusing capacity.

As regional localization of respiratory function in gut air-breathing fishes seems to be connected with "morphological remodeling" of the epithelium of their gut, the present research demonstrated the potential efficiency of the O. affinis stomach as a respiratory organ.

routes.route: skin / cutaneous surface used for aerial gas exchange
routes.anatomy: A thinned, highly vascularised epidermis with capillaries brought close to or into the epithelium. In the loach the respiratory capacity of skin is studied by regenerating it and sampling 'when their capillaries were the most abundant (the structural foundation of air-breathing in fish) during healing'. In mudskippers the skin is the amphibious exchange surface and is remodelled by air exposure: 'Histological analyses indicate transient epidermal remodeling and markers of oxidative stress'.
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Facultative and bimodal in loach; in mudskippers the skin is an obligatory part of an amphibious habit. Storz et al. describe the blue-spotted mudskipper as 'an amphibious, facultative air-breathing fish'.

genetics.what_is_shown: Expression and correlation only. Huang et al. compared regenerated skin of a cutaneous air-breathing loach against a water-breathing catfish and found a matrix-and-vessel programme: 'itga11, itga5, thbs2, thbs1, thbs4b, fn1, and rps6kb1 were up-regulated, whereas fgfr4, bmp3, and igfbp3 down-regulated upon skin regeneration; thbs3a, ngf, pdgfc, sost, bmp1, and angptl1 were up-regulated and then down-regulated, while chd and bmp2 presented opposite expression patterns', with fn1, itga5, loxl2a, loxl2b, lgals1 and plekhh1 validated by qPCR. In a mudskipper, air exposure drives 'differentially expressed genes significantly enriched in pathways associated with keratinization, hypoxia response, vascular morphogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling', with 'activation of the Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) signaling pathway during air exposure, with ... upregulation of c1qtnf7'. On the O2-transport side, mudskipper globin genetics gave a negative result: 'It therefore appears that the ability to switch between aquatic and aerial respiration does not necessarily require a division of labor between functionally distinct isoHbs with specialized oxygenation properties.' Comparative genomics of mudskipper versus tetrapods finds selection on 'immune responses, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, and kidney development' and 'convergent contraction of eight gene families, including beta-gamma-crystallin coding genes' - none of it on a respiratory surface. NO gene has been knocked out or overexpressed for cutaneous air breathing in any fish; the single functional test in this family of papers is fn1b in the barbel, not in the skin.
genetics.organism: Misgurnus anguillicaudatus, Pelteobagrus fulvidraco, Scartelaos histophorus, Boleophthalmus pectinirostris, Periophthalmus (comparative genomics)
genetics.experiment_type: RNA-seq of regenerated vs original skin, qPCR validation, histology, transcriptomics of air exposure and recovery, antioxidant enzyme assays, globin gene cluster synteny and O2-equilibrium measurement, positive-selection and gene-family (CAFE) analysis

costs_and_limits: DESICCATION is the governing limit and the animal pays for it behaviourally: 'During their low humidity exposure, frequency of the rolling behaviour and pectoral-fin movements increased by more than five times to moisten the skin before systemic dehydration.' A respiratory skin must be continuously rewetted, which means staying near water.

Air exposure injures the surface it breathes with: in Scartelaos histophorus air exposure produces 'transient epidermal remodeling and markers of oxidative stress, reflecting reversible cellular damage'; in aestivating Protopterus dolloi there is 'narrowing of epidermal layers and decrease of mucous cells' followed by 're-thickening of epidermal layers'.
The skin is not ventilated, so uptake cannot be increased on demand the way a bladder or chamber can be refilled faster; the only levers are surface area, barrier thickness and perfusion.
No source read here reports cutaneous CO2 excretion figures for a fish in air.

routes.route: buccal, buccopharyngeal, opercular or palatal epithelium used for aerial gas exchange (including simple air-bubble holding with no specialised surface)
routes.anatomy: Respiratory capillaries proliferate over the lining of the mouth, pharynx and opercular cavity. In swamp eels 'Both species use the buccopharyngeal cavity for aerial respiration', and the capillary architecture differs with dependence: 'The aerial respiratory capillaries are distributed with no particular pattern in O. bengalense, whereas the capillaries occur in clusters, each composed of repeatedly turning capillaries in M. albus.' In the electric eel the whole air-breathing organ is a capillary-rich buccal lining, and Ishimatsu overturns the textbook account of its supply: 'the entire aerial respiratory capillaries are perfused with the post-branchial blood, not with the pre-branchial blood as previously assumed.' At the low end of the route, some fishes simply hold a bubble with no specialisation at all: in Awaous tajasica 'Palate morphology did not reveal specialized respiratory structures, and only typical sensory structures such as taste buds were observed, indicating the absence of a dedicated aerial exchange surface.' In Gobionellus oceanicus 'the integument of the palate has a short diffusion barrier thickness and a large calculated O2-diffusion capacity suggesting that it functions as the ABO.'
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Graded within the route, and the gradient is the point: Ophisternon bengalense 'only infrequently breathes air when in hypoxic water', Monopterus albus 'is more strongly dependent on air-breathing', and the electric eel takes 80% of its O2 from air in normoxic water. Awaous tajasica and Gobionellus oceanicus are facultative, air-gulping only under hypoxia.

genetics.what_is_shown: NOTHING. No gene, expression programme, regulatory change or developmental route has been identified for buccal, buccopharyngeal, opercular or palatal aerial gas exchange in any fish, in any source read in this run. All four papers covering this route (Ishimatsu on Monopterus and Ophisternon, Ishimatsu on Electrophorus, Trevisan on Awaous, Aguilar on Gobionellus) are comparative vascular anatomy, stereology and respirometry with no molecular component. Genome assemblies exist for Monopterus (found in a search listing but not read in this run), but no study was found connecting any gene to the buccopharyngeal respiratory surface. This is the route with the largest anatomical literature and zero genetics.
genetics.experiment_type: n/a - vascular casting, histology, stereology, respirometry and behavioural observation only

costs_and_limits: Heavy reliance on air through this route does NOT drag the circulation toward a divided, lung-type design, which bears directly on how far a fish can go: 'These findings, when coupled with the fact that the electric eel obtains 80% of oxygen requirement from air in normoxic water, suggest that heavy reliance on air-breathing is not a driving force for the restructuring of the central cardiovascular system toward double circulation, in which oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is separated.' The electric eel's heart 'shows no anatomical specialization to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood'.
Capacity is capped by cavity volume: the organ is the mouth, and the fish must keep that mouth shut on a bubble, which conflicts with feeding and with ram ventilation.
At the unspecialised end the route works without any new structure at all - Awaous achieves 30% aerial uptake with no respiratory epithelium - but equally it cannot be scaled up without one.

Gill regression accompanies dependence (Monopterus has rudimentary filaments on three arches and a bypassed fourth arch), carrying the same ion, acid-base and nitrogen-excretion costs noted for the gas-bladder route.

routes.route: barbel used as an air-breathing organ
routes.anatomy: A sensory barbel carrying a central vascular axis brought very close to the surface: 'we find here for the first time a unique central vascular structure in the loach barbel, with a blood-gas diffusion distance as short as that of the posterior intestine'. The barrier is plastic: 'Under acute hypoxia, the distance of loach barbels became significantly shorter.'
routes.obligate_or_facultative: Facultative accessory organ in an otherwise facultative air breather.

genetics.what_is_shown: A loss-of-function test: 'We further generated an fn1b-depletion loach (MT for short) using the CRISPR/Cas9 technique. It was indicated that depletion of fn1b could weaker barbel air-breathing ability.' The gene was reached from a transcriptome of air-exposed barbels ('A total of 2546 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) ... were identified, and 13 key DEGs related to barbel air-breathing were screened out'), then placed by 'sequence, expression, and location analysis'. The organ itself was established functionally by ablation: barbel removal lowered air-breathing frequency. This is necessity, not mechanism: no interaction partner, pathway step or rescue is shown, and no gain-of-function.
genetics.experiment_type: RNA-seq of air-exposed vs control barbel, qPCR, in situ localisation, CRISPR/Cas9 depletion, barbel ablation, air-breathing-frequency assay, diffusion-distance histomorphometry

costs_and_limits: The paper's own selling point is that this organ is expendable: 'due to nonlethal and regenerative characteristics, the loach barbel ... can be a good model for fish air-breathing research' - i.e. its contribution is accessory, and removing it only reduces air-breathing frequency rather than killing the fish.
Surface area is tiny compared with the posterior intestine or a gas bladder, so the route cannot carry a large aerobic load.
A barbel in air is a bare, thin-barriered surface and so is the most exposed to desiccation of any route here; no source read quantified water loss from it.

costs_and_limits_across_routes: A barbel in air is a bare, thin-barriered surface and so is the most exposed to desiccation of any route here; no source read quantified water loss from it.

A gas bladder is a poor buoyancy device away from the surface: 'on descend from the water surface its contribution as a buoyancy device is very limited because the swimbladder is compressed by increasing hydrostatic pressure' (Pelster 2021).
A stomach full of air is a stomach not full of food; the digestive conflict documented for the loach hindgut applies by the same logic, but no source read here measured it for a gastric air breather.

Air exposure dries and remodels the integument even in an obligate lung breather: in aestivating Protopterus dolloi 'short-term aestivation induces major reorganization, with narrowing of epidermal layers and decrease of mucous cells', and 'aestivation correlates with an increased oxidative stress and changes of Heat Shock Proteins expression'.

Air exposure injures the surface it breathes with: in Scartelaos histophorus air exposure produces 'transient epidermal remodeling and markers of oxidative stress, reflecting reversible cellular damage'; in aestivating Protopterus dolloi there is 'narrowing of epidermal layers and decrease of mucous cells' followed by 're-thickening of epidermal layers'.
At the unspecialised end the route works without any new structure at all - Awaous achieves 30% aerial uptake with no respiratory epithelium - but equally it cannot be scaled up without one.

BUOYANCY CONFLICT, stated directly: 'Using the swimbladder as a buoyancy structure resulted in the loss of its function as an air-breathing organ and required the development of a gas secreting mechanism' (Pelster 2021). The two jobs are mutually exclusive in the erythrinids: the jeju uses the bladder for aerial respiration, the sister genus traira 'uses the swimbladder as a buoyancy organ and not for aerial oxygen uptake'.

Blocking access to air kills these fish faster than hypoxia itself does: 'Mortality in the restricted group was higher than those in the control and the hypoxic groups' (normoxic water, air breathing denied).
Blocking air breathing damages the organ: in the inhibited group 'Intraepithelial capillaries in posterior intestines of loaches from T05 were broken'.
Both uses require surfactant: 'As gas-filled cavities the respiratory swimbladder and the buoyancy device require surfactant' (Pelster 2021).

CO2 EXCRETION STAYS AQUATIC: aerial CO2 excretion is only 3-12% of total in Arapaima under normocapnia, and 'Because of the much greater diffusion constant of CO2 than O2 in water, the gills also remain important for CO2 release' (Fernandes 2012). Chitala ornata still excretes 79% and Pangasianodon 91% of CO2 to severely hypoxic water. The ABO can take over CO2 excretion (59-71% of total) only when the water itself is hypercapnic.
Capacity is capped by cavity volume: the organ is the mouth, and the fish must keep that mouth shut on a bubble, which conflicts with feeding and with ram ventilation.

DESICCATION is the governing limit and the animal pays for it behaviourally: 'During their low humidity exposure, frequency of the rolling behaviour and pectoral-fin movements increased by more than five times to moisten the skin before systemic dehydration.' A respiratory skin must be continuously rewetted, which means staying near water.

DIGESTION-RESPIRATION CONFLICT, the gut analogue of the buoyancy conflict: 'Results obtained here suggested an overlap of air-breathing and nutrient uptake function of posterior intestine in loach. Intestinal air-breathing inhibition in loach would influence the posterior intestine's nutrient uptake ability and endothelial capillary structure stability.' PEPT1a is absent from the respiratory hindgut altogether, so peptide uptake is given up in the respiratory zone.

beloniformes.finding: NOTHING IS KNOWN. There is no literature on air breathing, aerial gas exchange, a respiratory gas bladder, or the genetics of any respiratory surface in Beloniformes, and none at all for Exocoetidae. The family is represented in PubMed by 33 records and the four flying-fish genera queried by 53, and the intersection of either set with any respiration or swim-bladder term is empty. The nearest beloniform with any gas-bladder literature at all is the medaka Oryzias latipes, and that work treats the swim bladder purely as a buoyancy organ whose inflation is a developmental-toxicology endpoint (thyroid disruptors, metals), not as a gas-exchange surface. Consequently every statement in this file about how a fish breathes air is proxy data from another order: Osteoglossiformes (Arapaima, Heterotis, Chitala), Cypriniformes (Misgurnus), Siluriformes (Clarias, Pangasianodon, Pterygoplichthys, Otocinclus), Anabantiformes (Channa, Betta, Trichogaster, Anabas), Synbranchiformes (Monopterus), Gymnotiformes (Electrophorus), Gobiiformes (mudskippers, Awaous, Gobionellus), Polypteriformes, Dipnoi and Actinistia. For the flying fish itself the gas bladder is, on the evidence available, an unstudied organ: there is no measurement of its vascularity, barrier thickness, surfactant, or whether it is physostomous, and no expression or functional genetics of any kind.

gas_bladder_lung_homology.what_is_established: Homology of the gas bladder and the tetrapod lung is accepted and now supported at the level of cell types, but the molecular account of the SWITCH between them is incomplete and partly negative. (1) The organs are homologous and the diagnostic difference is budding direction: 'An important organismal trait of ray-finned fishes is the gas bladder, an air-filled organ that, in most fishes, functions for buoyancy control, and is homologous to the lungs of lobe-finned fishes. The critical morphological difference between lungs and gas bladders, which otherwise share many characteristics, is the general direction of budding during development. Lungs bud ventrally and the gas bladder buds dorsally from the anterior foregut.' (2) Cell-type transcriptomes agree: 'our data indicate broad homology between the swim bladder of ray-finned fishes (here, the zebrafish) and the lungs of tetrapods and the West African lungfish', and 'epithelial cells and granulocyte cells of the lung and swim bladder show high similarity among these four species, suggesting that these cell types share ancestral cell types'. 49 genes with a ZFIN swim-bladder-development phenotype also show cell-type-specific expression in the lungfish lung. (3) Bulk transcriptomes had already shown the same: 'we established the resemblance of transcriptome of the zebrafish swimbladder and mammalian lungs'. (4) The surfactant system is shared and phylogenetically old: SP-A-immunoreactive protein is present in carp swim bladder and intestine but not gills, gas gland cells carry lamellar bodies and produce surfactant, and in zebrafish bloc1s1 is required for the swimbladder surfactant gene programme. (5) The developmental-genetic account of the dorsal-versus-ventral switch is the weak point and the key result is NEGATIVE: the tetrapod lung regulators Nkx2.1 and Sox2 are conserved in bichir LUNG development but their gas-bladder expression 'are inconsistent with the hypothesis that they regulate the direction of gas bladder budding'; Bmp4, ventral in lung, 'is not expressed' in the developing gas bladder, and the authors fall back on a hypothesis that the Actinopteri-specific paralogue Bmp16 'was recruited to regulate gas bladder development in the Actinopteri in place of Bmp4'. (6) The ancestral lung is the primitive state within bony fishes: 'primitive lungs, which originated from the respiratory pharynx and were located on the ventral side of the alimentary tracts, can be observed in several extant basal actinopterygians (bichirs, reedfish) and all extant sarcopterygians, as well as some fossils of coelacanths', and 'The lung of ray-finned fishes was replaced (but retained by bichirs and the reedfish of the basal order Polypteriformes) by an air-breathing swim bladder still present in holostei fishes (the bowfin and gars) that was further repurposed by teleost fishes to facilitate buoyancy'. That last sentence is the crux for this project: in teleosts, the lineage containing flying fishes, the organ has already been repurposed away from respiration.
gas_bladder_lung_homology.evidence_grade_note: The homology claim rests on morphology, shared cell types and correlated transcriptomes (association). The one piece at a higher grade is tangential to homology itself: bloc1s1 is required for the swimbladder surfactant programme in zebrafish (necessity). The budding-direction mechanism is explicitly unresolved and its leading candidate (Bmp16) is labelled a hypothesis by its own authors.

physics_confirms_the_requirement.what_it_changes: With the oxygen chain wired, the physics thread's flier climbs at 2.8 m/s to 179 m and its flight power collapses at 66 seconds when the burst store empties, while the blood oxygen store is still at 35%. The store cannot be drawn on because gills do not ventilate in air. So the air-breathing surface is not an optional refinement of this design: without it the animal is, in the physics thread's words, 'a jumper with a long ballistic-plus-burst arc'.

what_is_missing: A gas bladder used for respiration conflicts with its use for buoyancy, which is a design cost, not a gene.

how_to_read_this: A route is listed because an experiment changed the parameter, never because a gene sounds relevant.
Evidence grades are the project's five: association, necessity, sufficiency, mechanism, hypothesis.
An effect size appears only where a paper gives a number; most of this literature reports morphology in figures.
Pleiotropy is attached to every gene from the vetted map, because every lever here moves more than the fin.
Stage regimes do not interpolate: a larval fin measurement is not an adult fin.
